messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Animals: Dogs, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Priya is a 61-year-old South Asian woman who immigrated to the Central Valley of California decades ago, where she has spent most of her adult life working the fields alongside her husband. She is soft-spoken and deliberate in her speech, and it took her several sessions before she could describe what happened to her in anything approaching full detail. What she eventually disclosed was this: approximately fourteen months ago, she was working alone at the edge of an irrigation ditch at dusk, waiting for a co-worker who never arrived, when a man she recognized vaguely from a neighboring property attacked her. He came from behind, and the assault happened on the ground, in the dirt, with a farm dog barking somewhere nearby — a sound that continued throughout. She did not scream. She told herself afterward, and then told herself again, that she had simply frozen, though she has spent the months since trying to understand what that means about her.

In the weeks that followed, Priya said very little to anyone. She returned to work because the family needed her income and because stopping felt, in some way she could not articulate, like admitting that something permanent had happened. But the fields had changed. The same low light at the end of a shift, the same smell of turned earth, the same sound of a dog from a neighboring property — any of these could bring the full memory back without the slightest warning, not as a recollection but as an event happening in real time, her body pressed into the ground again, the weight and the sound and the particular quality of the fading sky above her. She described this to her therapist as "the film that plays again," and she said it plays whether she wants it to or not. There is no distance in it. When it comes, she is there.

She had come to believe that her body understood danger in a way her mind no longer trusted. Before she could register that a co-worker had placed a hand on her shoulder to get her attention, she would be on her feet, heart hammering, several steps away. She was certain that something in her had been rewired, that her reactions were no longer under her control, and this frightened her almost as much as the memory itself. At night she lay awake listening — to her husband's breathing, to sounds from the road, to nothing in particular — because sleep felt like a surrender of the only vigilance she had left.

Her marriage had quietly hollowed out over the course of the year. Her husband, a patient and gentle man by her account, had tried more than once to be close to her, and each time she had withdrawn so completely that he had eventually stopped trying. She had not explained why. She did not know how to explain it without explaining everything, and she was not ready for that. What frightened her most about intimacy now was not the act itself but the way it collapsed time — the way closeness could make the memory present again in an instant. The distance between them had grown into something neither of them named, and Priya carried a private grief about this that she had not shared with anyone before coming to therapy.

Dogs remained a particular problem. The agricultural work she depends on puts her in proximity to farm dogs almost daily, and she had begun arriving earlier in the morning and leaving before the neighboring property's dog was let out, rearranging her schedule in ways her employer had noticed and questioned. She had offered vague explanations. The reorganization of her days around a single animal had cost her hours and a degree of professional standing she had built over many years.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a conversation with her daughter, who lives nearby and had noticed the changes in her mother's face and manner. Her daughter said simply that she was scared for her, and Priya had cried for the first time since the assault. She came to therapy the following week. What she is most hoping for, she said quietly in the first session, is to be able to stand in a field at dusk again without leaving herself.
